pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Types of Fossils (ages 7–9): distinguish BODY fossils (preserved parts of the organism — bones, teeth, shells) from TRACE fossils (evidence of activity — footprints, trackways, eggs, burrows, coprolites/dung), and explain what each type reveals.
• Standards — UK (DfE): builds on Y3 'Rocks' (fossils as remains of living things) and 'working scientifically' (identify, classify, and use evidence); the body/trace distinction is the organising idea for reading fossils.
• Standards — US (NGSS): supports grade-3 3-LS4-1 (interpret fossil evidence about organisms AND their behaviours/environments) and the MS fossil-record strand.
• Operational details — The key idea is that the TWO types answer different questions: body fossils tell us what an animal LOOKED LIKE (anatomy — size, shape, teeth); trace fossils tell us how it BEHAVED (how it moved, what it ate, where it nested). Have children sort examples and, crucially, say what each could tell a scientist. Watch the boundary cases: an egg or a tooth-marked bone; a coprolite is a trace (activity) even though it's a solid object. This classification is the springboard to the next topics (trackways, coprolites) and to the domain's evidence-reasoning spine.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~7): sorts clear examples into body vs trace. Tier B (~8): explains body fossils show appearance and trace fossils show behaviour, with an example of each. Tier C (~9): classifies tricky cases (eggs, dung, burrows) correctly and states a specific inference each type supports.
bestPractices: Organise around the guiding question 'part of the animal, or something it DID?' to make the body/trace cut usable.
Always pair the sort with 'what could this tell us?' so classification connects to inference, not just labelling.
Use boundary cases (eggs, coprolites, burrows) deliberately — they force students to apply the rule rather than pattern-match to 'bone = fossil'.
Contrast the questions each answers: anatomy (body) vs behaviour (trace), so students see why both matter.
Connect forward: trace fossils (tracks, dung) are the evidence base for the following behaviour topics.
keyRepresentations: A two-column sorter: BODY (bones, teeth, shells) vs TRACE (footprints, eggs, burrows, dung).
A 'what it tells us' tag on each example (looks vs behaviour).
Paired icons: a skeleton (body) beside a footprint (trace) to anchor the contrast.
Boundary-case cards (egg, coprolite) that prompt applying the rule.
commonMisconceptions: 'Only bones/body parts are fossils' — footprints, burrows, eggs, and dung are trace fossils too.
'A coprolite (dung) is a body fossil because it's a solid lump' — it records activity, so it's a trace fossil.
'Trace fossils are less useful' — they uniquely reveal behaviour (speed, diet, nesting) body fossils can't.
'A footprint contains the foot' — a trace fossil is the mark/impression, not the body part itself.
'You can tell everything from one fossil' — anatomy and behaviour usually need different fossil types combined.

learn.summary: For ages 7–9 learning Types of Fossils: children distinguish BODY fossils (preserved parts of an organism — bones, teeth, shells, which reveal anatomy/appearance) from TRACE fossils (evidence of activity — footprints, trackways, eggs, burrows, coprolites/dung, which reveal behaviour like movement, diet, nesting). The core task is to classify WITH REASON: for each find, decide 'part of the animal, or something it DID?' and then say what it could tell a scientist. Boundary cases (eggs, coprolites, burrows) and combining both fossil types to reconstruct a scene are central. (Eggs are used here as the source's worked boundary case, read as TRACE via nesting behaviour; eggshell itself is a genuinely debatable case.)

activities.title: Fossil-sorting bench: part of the animal, or something it did?
feedback: If a learner sorts the coprolite as a body fossil because it is a solid lump, prompt 'part of the animal, or something it DID?' — dung is produced by an action (eating), so it is a trace fossil, and it happens to reveal what the animal ate.
If a learner treats a footprint as a piece of the foot, distinguish the impression left in mud from the foot itself: the trace is a record of an action, not a preserved body part.
If a learner says a footprint 'isn't really a fossil', widen the definition — a footprint turned to rock is as much a fossil as a bone; it just records activity rather than anatomy.

When the learner correctly assigns an inference (tooth → diet and appearance; footprint → how it moved, or, with several trackways side by side, whether animals travelled in a group), confirm that they have linked the category to what it can tell a scientist, not just applied a label.

For the egg, keep the trace reading tied to nesting behaviour rather than presenting it as the only possible answer: the eggshell is a preserved structure, but as a clutch/nest it records nesting, which is why it is read here as a trace.
activities.rationale: The target is a classify-with-reason skill, so pairing each sort with 'what could this tell us?' connects classification to inference rather than labelling. Deliberately including boundary cases (egg, coprolite, burrow) forces learners to apply the guiding rule instead of pattern-matching 'bone = fossil'. Ending by fusing a body fossil with trace fossils shows the two types answering different questions together. Dragging finds along a belt and a discovery panel that reconstructs a scene are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required.
sourceClaims: Body fossils preserve parts of the organism (bones, teeth, shells) and reveal anatomy; trace fossils record activity (footprints, trackways, burrows, eggs, coprolites) and reveal behaviour such as movement, diet, and nesting.
learnerActions: Work through a set of fossil finds one at a time: a tooth, a shell, a footprint, an egg, a coiled burrow, and a knobbly lump of dung (coprolite).

For each find, answer two questions in order: first 'Is this a part of the animal, or something it DID?' (sorting it into BODY or TRACE); then 'So what can it tell us?' (what it looked like, or how it behaved).
Place the tooth and shell into BODY and tag them 'what it looked like'; place the footprint into TRACE and tag it 'how it moved'.

Tackle the tricky boundary cases deliberately: decide that a solid lump of dung records an action (eating), so it is a TRACE fossil that reveals diet; discuss where an egg belongs (read here as a record of nesting behaviour, a TRACE reading) and where a burrow belongs and why.

Finish by combining the two types: use a body fossil to give a dinosaur its shape, then footprints and dung that scientists think came from that kind of dinosaur to show how it moved (for example, widely spaced prints suggesting running) and what it ate — stating what each fossil type contributed.
activities.intendedInsight: Body fossils and trace fossils answer two different questions — what an animal looked like versus what it did — and the richest reconstructions combine both. A fossil need not be a body part: a mark or product of activity turned to rock (footprint, dung) is still a fossil.

activities.title: Tappable fossil gallery: two shelves, two kinds of evidence
feedback: Use the paired icons of a skeleton (body) beside a footprint (trace) to anchor the contrast if the two categories blur.
Draw attention to the 'what it reveals' tag so the learner links the type to the information it carries, not just the picture.
activities.rationale: A captioned gallery introduces the distinction clearly and makes the anatomy-vs-behaviour contrast visible. On its own it presents the categories rather than requiring the learner to apply the rule to boundary cases, so it works best as a scaffold before the sorting-with-reason task.
sourceClaims: Body fossils preserve parts of the organism (bones, teeth, shells) and reveal anatomy; trace fossils record activity (footprints, trackways, burrows, eggs, coprolites) and reveal behaviour such as movement, diet, and nesting.
learnerActions: Explore two labelled shelves of specimens — one BODY shelf (bones, teeth, shells) and one TRACE shelf (footprints, eggs/nests, burrows, dung).

Tap each specimen to reveal its type and a 'what it reveals' caption (anatomy/appearance for body; behaviour such as movement, diet or nesting for trace — e.g. the egg/nest read as evidence of nesting).
After browsing, state in your own words how the two shelves answer different questions.
activities.intendedInsight: Body fossils reveal what an animal looked like; trace fossils reveal what it did — each category carries a different kind of information.

activities.title: Classify and match check: body/trace and what it reveals
feedback: Correct answer: the footprint is a trace fossil recording something the animal did (how it moved; a longer trackway can also suggest how fast it went, and several trackways together whether animals travelled in a group); the tooth is a body fossil showing what its body was like and giving clues to its diet.
If a learner sorts into two piles but cannot say what each reveals, revisit the 'what it tells us' tags before moving on — sorting without the inference is only partial understanding.
If a learner assigns both objects to 'what it looked like', use trackways, nests and dung to show behaviour is recoverable from trace fossils.
activities.rationale: Categorisation and matching give a clean check against the objective and surface the common errors (rejecting footprints as fossils, treating a footprint as a body part, denying behaviour is knowable). This confirms rather than builds the reasoning, so it suits a checkpoint after the sorting-with-reason work.
sourceClaims: Body fossils preserve parts of the organism (bones, teeth, shells) and reveal anatomy; trace fossils record activity (footprints, trackways, burrows, eggs, coprolites) and reveal behaviour such as movement, diet, and nesting.
learnerActions: Sort a mix of examples into a BODY pile and a TRACE pile (e.g. bones, teeth, shells vs footprints, nests, dung).
Match each fossil to what it reveals: fossil → anatomy (what it looked like) or fossil → behaviour (how it moved, ate, nested).

Answer this question: a palaeontologist finds a fossilised footprint and a fossilised tooth — which tells you how the dinosaur behaved, and which tells you what its body was like? Explain how you decided.
activities.intendedInsight: Confirm you can both place a fossil in the right category and state the specific inference it supports.

activities.title: Palaeontologist's question game: part or action?
feedback: If the learner cannot say why a coprolite is a trace fossil, steer back to whether it is a preserved body part or the product of an action.
Press gently on 'how fast could it run from the skeleton alone?' to surface that movement speed is a behaviour, most directly read from trackways rather than from a body fossil.
activities.rationale: Socratic questioning suits the reasoning goal because it demands justification. A self-paced sorting bench may be more reliable for independent practice at this age, so use the question game to deepen or assess reasoning rather than as the sole first exposure.
learnerActions: Take finds handed over one by one by a palaeontologist (role-played by a teacher, peer, or on-screen character).
For each, classify it as body or trace and justify out loud using 'part of the animal, or something it did?'.

Respond to follow-up probes such as: what could a fossilised nest of eggs tell you that a leg bone never could? Is a coprolite a body or trace fossil, and why? Could you work out how fast a dinosaur ran from its skeleton alone?
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to justify a classification aloud — and reason about what each fossil type can and cannot reveal — shows the rule is understood, not just memorised.

constraints: The body/trace distinction is categorical, not spatial — a 3D model does not help decide whether a fossil is body or trace for this objective, so prefer sorting and reasoning tasks over spatial manipulation here (scoped to this classification, not a universal claim about 3D for the topic).
A captioned gallery introduces and presents the distinction but does not itself require the learner to apply the rule to boundary cases; treat it as a scaffold, not the assessment of understanding.
Categorisation and matching checks can confirm the distinction but do not themselves elicit the justification; pair them with explanation tasks so learners state what each type reveals.

Deliberately include boundary cases (eggs, coprolites, burrows) — without them, learners can pattern-match 'bone = fossil' without grasping the rule. Keep the egg's trace reading tied to nesting behaviour, since eggshell as a structure is itself a debatable case.
Always pair each sort with 'what could this tell us?' so classification connects to inference; sorting into piles without stating what each type reveals is only partial mastery.

Keep the point that trace fossils are not less useful — they record behaviour directly (how fast and in what way an animal moved, what it actually ate, how it nested) in ways body fossils usually cannot. Body fossils such as teeth can still suggest diet, and the fullest reconstructions combine both.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the single source (Natural History Museum UK / USGS body-vs-trace pages) is marked verified:false and was not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The single sourced claim supports the body/trace anatomy-vs-behaviour distinction; it does not establish the comparative efficacy of any particular activity format (sorting bench vs gallery vs conversation). Format preferences here are pedagogical proposals, not evidence of superiority.

The original claim that '3D adds no help' has been narrowed to a scoped statement that this classification is categorical rather than spatial; no source establishes that 3D is universally unhelpful for the topic.

Egg classification: the original and its source treat eggs as TRACE fossils (nesting behaviour). This is used here as a deliberate, behaviour-framed teaching boundary case, but eggshell itself is a genuinely debatable case (a preserved mineralised structure can read as a body fossil). The placement is retained as source-faithful, not independently verified, and is not presented to learners as the only defensible answer without the nesting framing.

Self-audit: coprolite classification (trace, not body) is internally consistent — it records an action despite being a solid object; a footprint is an impression, not a preserved foot. No arithmetic or physics claims are present. Assessment/quiz-step vocabulary was removed from learner-facing prompts, and the check activity's intended insight no longer references a burrow case absent from that activity.

probeDeeper: What could a fossilised nest of eggs tell you that a leg bone never could?
Is a coprolite — fossilised dung — a body fossil or a trace fossil? Why?
Could you work out how fast a dinosaur could run from its skeleton alone?
assess.correctAnswer: The footprint is a trace fossil — it records something the animal did (how it moved, how fast, whether it was in a group). The tooth is a body fossil — a preserved part of the animal that shows what its body was like (and its diet). Trace fossils record activity; body fossils record the organism itself.

errorPatterns.pattern: Only bones and teeth are 'real' fossils: 'a footprint isn't a fossil.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Widen the definition of fossil to include preserved traces of activity; a footprint turned to rock is as much a fossil as a bone.
errorPatterns.distractor: The tooth is the only real fossil — a footprint isn't a fossil.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Dismisses the footprint as not a fossil, or insists the tooth is the only fossil that counts.

errorPatterns.pattern: A trace fossil is a preserved body part: 'the footprint tells you about its body because a footprint is part of its foot.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish the mark left in mud from the foot itself; the trace is a record of an action, not a body part.
errorPatterns.distractor: The footprint tells you about its body, because a footprint is a piece of its foot.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats the footprint as a fossilised foot rather than an impression left behind.

errorPatterns.pattern: Fossils only tell us what animals looked like, not what they did.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use trackways/nests/dung to show behaviour is recoverable from trace fossils.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies that behaviour is knowable from fossils; assigns both objects to 'what it looked like.'

responseLevels.gap: Thinks only bones and teeth are fossils and rejects footprints, eggs or dung as fossils at all.
responseLevels.full: Sorts correctly AND explains body fossils show what the animal was like while trace fossils show what it did, transferring the distinction to a novel case such as eggs or a burrow.
responseLevels.partial: Sorts examples into a body pile and a trace pile but cannot explain what each type reveals — that body fossils show physical form and trace fossils show behaviour.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A palaeontologist finds a fossilised dinosaur footprint and a fossilised dinosaur tooth. Which one tells you how the dinosaur behaved, and which tells you what its body was like? Explain how you decided.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who believes only bones and teeth count says the footprint 'isn't really a fossil.' A child who holds the two categories maps behaviour to the trace fossil and body/appearance to the body fossil, and can justify why.

sources.claim: Body fossils preserve parts of the organism (bones, teeth, shells) and reveal anatomy; trace fossils record activity (footprints, trackways, burrows, eggs, coprolites) and reveal behaviour such as movement, diet, and nesting.
